findings.subject: First Constituent Congress in former Jesuit church
findings.assertion: On 24 February 1822 the First Constituent Congress convened in the former church of San Pedro y San Pablo; on 21 May Iturbide took the oath there as emperor, while the coronation was held at the Cathedral.

findings.subject: Federal constitution and national legislature
findings.assertion: UNAM locates the Second Constituent Congress and the 4 October 1824 federal constitution promulgation at San Pedro y San Pablo; the legislature remained there until the 1829 move to the National Palace.

findings.subject: Lerdo Law rental-capitalization mechanism
findings.assertion: The 1856 Lerdo Law directed that certain corporate properties rented to tenants be adjudicated at a capital value derived from annual rent calculated at 6 percent; unleased eligible properties went to auction. These are provisions of law, not proof of individual implementation.

findings.subject: Civil institutions and exceptions in Lerdo Law
findings.assertion: The 1856 law applied to civil corporations including municipalities and schools, but article 8 exempted institutional direct-use buildings and municipal lands devoted exclusively to public services. It did not itself command universal demolition of convents.

findings.subject: Contemporary episcopal resistance
findings.assertion: On 26 July 1856 Bishop Clemente de Jesús Munguía protested the Lerdo Law as forced sales to specified buyers and argued Church property rights were independent of state authorization; this documents his partisan position, not the truth of his legal contention.

findings.subject: Juárez nationalization and separation
findings.assertion: On 12 July 1859 the Juárez government decreed that property administered by regular and secular clergy would enter the national domain and declared institutional separation of state and church. Its legal mechanism was distinct from the 1856 tenant-adjudication regime.
findings.locator: Nationalization Law articles 1 and 3; compare 1856 articles 1–2

findings.subject: Inventory rules for religious cultural objects
findings.assertion: The 1859 law assigned sacred vessels, liturgical vestments and images of suppressed orders to diocesan bishops under formal inventory while directing manuscripts, books, paintings and antiquities to public collections. Actual transfer of any particular object still requires separate evidence.

findings.subject: 1859 distinction between male and female communities
findings.assertion: The nationalization law suppressed male regular orders but permitted existing women's convents to continue. Exclaustrated nuns were to recover their dowries; mendicant nuns without dowries were promised 500 pesos. The later 1863 expulsion was a distinct measure.

findings.subject: 1865 imperial law did not blanket-reverse liberal property changes
findings.assertion: Maximilian's decree of 26 February 1865 ordered review of transactions under the 1856 and 1859 laws, confirmed those made legally and authorized invalidation or rehabilitation of others, with certain latter cases subject to a 25 percent payment.

findings.subject: 1865 protection for certain women's property rights
findings.assertion: Article 9 of the 1865 imperial review decree rejected certain renunciations by women owning no other real property and by guardians on behalf of minors. This is a statutory restriction; actual enforcement has not been researched.

findings.subject: San Francisco convent subdivision reshaped streets
findings.assertion: INAH reports that the Reforma-era division of the San Francisco complex opened the street connections associated with present-day Gante and 16 de Septiembre; former convent spaces were later used for a circus, stables, hotel and Protestant worship.

findings.subject: Multi-era civic use of San Pedro y San Pablo
findings.assertion: UNAM traces the former church's use as a military college in 1858–1860, later school/hospital/warehouse uses, its 1920–21 restoration and murals, and its role as National Newspaper Library from 1944 through 1979.
